cosmic: place in the universe at large
places in the universe at large

places.name: the Milky Way
places.fact: About 200 billion stars. Arms, bar and our place in the Orion Spur follow radio and Gaia maps; nobody has ever seen it from outside.
places.type: barred spiral galaxy · our home, 100,000 light-years across
readout: the Sun circles the centre at 230 km/s
one lap, a "galactic year", takes about 230 million years

places.name: Large Magellanic Cloud
places.fact: A small galaxy orbiting ours, bright enough to see by eye from the southern hemisphere. Its Tarantula Nebula is the most active star factory in the Local Group.
places.type: barred irregular galaxy · satellite of the Milky Way
readout: 163,000 light-years away · 1/10 the Milky Way's mass
host of SN 1987A, the nearest supernova in 400 years

places.name: Small Magellanic Cloud
places.fact: A dwarf galaxy being torn apart by the Large Magellanic Cloud and the Milky Way, trailing a bridge of gas and young stars behind it.
places.type: dwarf irregular galaxy · satellite of the Milky Way
readout: 200,000 light-years away · a few hundred million stars

places.name: Triangulum Galaxy
places.fact: A loose, flocculent spiral full of giant star-forming regions. On a dark night it is the most distant thing some people can see with the naked eye.
places.type: spiral galaxy · third-largest in the Local Group
readout: 2.73 million light-years · ~40 billion stars
may be a satellite of Andromeda

places.name: Sagittarius Dwarf
places.fact: Hidden behind the crowded middle of the Milky Way, it was found only in 1994. Our galaxy is tearing it into a stream of stars that loops right around the sky, and the globular cluster M54 sits at its heart.
places.type: dwarf spheroidal galaxy · being torn apart by the Milky Way
readout: 86,000 light-years, beyond the Milky Way's centre
half its light lies within 8,500 light-years

places.name: Fornax Dwarf
places.fact: Found by Harlow Shapley in 1938, it holds six globular clusters of its own. The brightest was seen by John Herschel in 1835, a century before the galaxy itself.
places.type: dwarf spheroidal galaxy · satellite of the Milky Way
readout: 465,000 light-years · 6 globular clusters of its own
as bright as 19 million Suns

places.name: Sculptor Dwarf
places.fact: The first dwarf spheroidal galaxy ever found, reported by Harlow Shapley in 1938 from photographs taken in South Africa. Most of its stars are more than 10 billion years old.
places.type: dwarf spheroidal galaxy · satellite of the Milky Way
readout: 274,000 light-years · found in 1938
half its light lies within 980 light-years

places.name: Leo I
places.fact: It lies a third of a degree north of Regulus, the bright star at the heart of Leo, whose glare makes it hard to see. One of the Milky Way's most distant satellites, it swung past our galaxy about a billion years ago.
places.type: dwarf spheroidal galaxy · one of the Milky Way's most distant satellites
readout: 830,000 light-years · 0.34° from the star Regulus
passed closest to the Milky Way about 1 billion years ago

places.name: Draco Dwarf
places.fact: Its stars move so fast that the galaxy must be held together by far more mass than they have. For every Sun's worth of light it holds about 100 Suns' worth of mass or more, so it is a favourite place to hunt for signs of dark matter.
places.type: dwarf spheroidal galaxy · satellite of the Milky Way
readout: 266,000 light-years · as bright as 300,000 Suns
about 100 Suns of mass for each Sun of light

places.name: Barnard's Galaxy
places.fact: E. E. Barnard found it in 1884. In 1925 Edwin Hubble measured its Cepheid stars and showed it lies far outside the Milky Way, one of the first proofs that other galaxies exist.
places.type: barred dwarf irregular galaxy · Local Group
readout: 1.5 million light-years · found by Barnard in 1884
Hubble's 1925 estimate: 700,000 light-years

places.name: IC 1613
places.fact: Max Wolf found it in 1906. We see it through a clear patch of our own galaxy and it holds little dust, so astronomers use its stars to check the rungs of the cosmic distance ladder.
places.type: dwarf irregular galaxy · Local Group
readout: 2.4 million light-years · found by Max Wolf in 1906
as bright as about 90 million Suns

places.name: Wolf-Lundmark-Melotte
places.fact: A lonely galaxy at the edge of the Local Group that seems never to have met another galaxy. Max Wolf found it in 1909, and in 2022 the James Webb Space Telescope photographed its stars to read its history.
places.type: dwarf irregular galaxy · on the edge of the Local Group
readout: 3.2 million light-years · at the Local Group's edge
the Webb telescope photographed its stars in 2022

places.name: Bode's Galaxy
places.fact: A textbook spiral whose arms were stirred up by a close pass with its neighbour M82 about 300 million years ago.
places.type: grand-design spiral
readout: 11.8 million light-years · 250 billion stars

places.name: Cigar Galaxy
places.fact: Forming stars ten times faster than the Milky Way. Supernova-driven winds blast red filaments of hydrogen out of both faces of the disk.
places.type: starburst galaxy
readout: 11.4 million light-years · a starburst triggered by M81

places.name: Pinwheel Galaxy
places.fact: Nearly twice the width of the Milky Way, seen almost face-on, its lopsided arms studded with more than 3,000 star-forming regions.
places.type: face-on spiral
readout: 20.9 million light-years · 170,000 light-years across

places.name: Sombrero Galaxy
places.fact: A huge glowing bulge ringed by a dark lane of dust. It hosts about 2,000 globular clusters and a billion-solar-mass black hole.
places.type: spiral seen nearly edge-on
readout: 31 million light-years · 50,000 light-years across

places.name: Centaurus A
places.fact: A giant elliptical still digesting a spiral galaxy it swallowed. Its black hole fires jets a million light-years long.
places.type: elliptical galaxy with a swallowed spiral
readout: 12 million light-years · the nearest radio galaxy

places.name: the cosmic web
places.fact: Galaxies gather into clusters strung along filaments hundreds of millions of light-years long, around voids. The famous clusters and voids here are at their real positions; the web between them is a statistical model.
places.type: filaments of galaxies around vast empty voids
readout: each dot is a galaxy · the Milky Way sits in the Laniakea supercluster
the Boötes Void, 330 million ly across, is almost empty

places.name: the observable universe
places.fact: A sphere 93 billion light-years across centred on us. Its edge is the cosmic microwave background, the afterglow of the Big Bang released 380,000 years after it began. (The pattern is illustrative.)
places.type: everything light has had time to reach us from, in 13.8 billion years
readout: about 2 trillion galaxies · edge 46.5 billion light-years away
the universe has expanded while the light was on its way

places.name: the Sun
places.fact: A million Earths would fit inside. Its visible surface boils with convection cells, dark sunspots and looping prominences of glowing hydrogen.
places.type: G2V main-sequence star · our star
readout: surface 5,500 °C, core 15 million °C · 1.39 million km across
light from its core takes ~100,000 years to reach the surface
drawn warm like a filtered photo · from space it looks white

places.name: the Solar System
places.fact: Planets shown where they are today, on their true orbits. The asteroid belt hides gaps carved by Jupiter; two swarms of Trojans share its orbit.
places.type: our planetary system · 8 planets, 5 dwarf planets, millions of small bodies
readout: Neptune orbits 30 AU out · light takes 4 hours to get there
Voyager 1, our farthest probe, is ~172 AU away after 49 years

places.name: the Oort cloud
places.fact: Trillions of comet nuclei surround the Sun out to a light-year or more, a third of the way to the nearest star. None has ever been seen directly.
places.type: shell of icy bodies · source of long-period comets
readout: outer edge ~100,000 AU (1.6 light-years)
a comet from here takes millions of years per orbit

places.name: Mercury
places.fact: A scorched, cratered world with almost no air: 430 °C by day, −180 °C at night. Its year is shorter than two of its own days.
places.type: rocky planet · closest to the Sun
readout: radius 2,440 km · 0.39 AU from the Sun
one solar day lasts 176 Earth days

places.name: Venus
places.fact: Almost Earth's twin in size, smothered by clouds of sulphuric acid. The surface is 465 °C under 92 times Earth's air pressure.
places.type: rocky planet · runaway greenhouse
readout: radius 6,052 km · spins backwards, once every 243 days
its cloud tops race around in just 4 days
cloud patterns drawn as ultraviolet photos show them: to the eye Venus looks plain

places.name: Mars
places.fact: Rust-red dust, polar ice caps, Olympus Mons (three times the height of Everest) and a canyon as long as the United States.
places.type: rocky planet · the red planet
readout: radius 3,390 km · a day lasts 24 h 37 min
surface pressure under 1% of Earth's

places.name: Uranus
places.fact: Knocked over by an ancient collision, it rolls around the Sun with its axis tilted 98°, so each pole gets 42 years of daylight.
places.type: ice giant · tipped on its side
readout: radius 25,360 km · 19 AU from the Sun
light from the Sun takes 2 h 40 min to arrive

places.name: Neptune
places.fact: The windiest world known: storms race at 2,000 km/h around a deep-blue methane atmosphere. It takes 165 years to orbit the Sun once.
places.type: ice giant · outermost planet
readout: radius 24,620 km · 30 AU from the Sun
found in 1846 by mathematics before telescopes

places.name: Pluto
places.fact: A world of nitrogen glaciers, water-ice mountains and a vast pale heart, seen close up only once, by New Horizons in 2015.
places.type: dwarf planet · Kuiper belt
readout: radius 1,188 km, smaller than our Moon
sunlight there is 1,000 times dimmer than at Earth

places.name: Earth
places.fact: The only world known to have life. Real coastlines, weather systems pushed by the trade winds and westerlies, city lights on the night side and auroras over the poles.
places.type: rocky planet · home
readout: radius 6,371 km · 71% ocean · 1 day = 23 h 56 min
~10,000 satellites now circle it

places.name: the Moon
places.fact: Born from a giant impact 4.5 billion years ago. The dark "seas" are ancient lava plains; bright rays splash out from young craters like Tycho.
places.type: Earth's natural satellite
readout: radius 1,737 km · 384,400 km from Earth
always shows us the same face; 12 people have walked on it

places.name: Jupiter
places.fact: Over twice the mass of all the other planets combined. The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has raged for at least 190 years.
places.type: gas giant · largest planet
readout: radius 71,492 km · a day lasts 9 h 56 min
winds up to 600 km/h between the bands

places.name: Io
places.fact: The most volcanic world known. Tidal squeezing by Jupiter melts its interior, feeding hundreds of volcanoes and lava lakes.
places.type: moon of Jupiter
readout: radius 1,822 km · 400 active volcanoes
plumes of sulphur rise 400 km into space

places.name: Europa
places.fact: A shell of ice cracked into long red streaks, floating on a global ocean holding twice the water of Earth's seas.
places.type: moon of Jupiter
readout: radius 1,561 km · ice shell 15 to 25 km thick
one of the best places to look for life

places.name: Ganymede
places.fact: The largest moon in the Solar System, wider than the planet Mercury but with less than half its mass. It is the only moon known to make its own magnetic field, and a salty ocean lies buried under its ice.
places.type: moon of Jupiter
readout: radius 2,631 km · 8% wider than the planet Mercury
its own magnetic field, found by the Galileo probe in 1996

places.name: Callisto
places.fact: The most heavily cratered world in the Solar System, almost as wide as Mercury. Its dark, icy surface has barely changed in billions of years, and a salty ocean may lie deep beneath it.
places.type: moon of Jupiter
readout: radius 2,410 km · 99% as wide as the planet Mercury
Valhalla, its biggest impact, has rings 3,000 km across

places.name: Sagittarius A*
places.fact: Its event horizon is 17 times wider than the Sun. Light skimming past bends into a ring; the approaching side of the disk glows brighter and bluer. Its real feeding disk is dimmer than shown.
places.type: supermassive black hole · 4.3 million Suns · heart of the Milky Way
readout: event horizon 25 million km across, 17 Suns wide
inner disk edge 3 r_s, orbiting at half the speed of light

places.name: S2 and the S-stars
places.fact: Tracking these stars for 30 years proved Sgr A* is a black hole (Nobel Prize 2020). S2 swings within 120 AU of it every 16 years, reaching 2.5% of light speed.
places.type: stars orbiting the black hole · proof it exists
readout: S2: 16-year orbit shown in 20 seconds
at closest approach 7,650 km/s; its light is visibly reddened by gravity

places.name: the Galactic Centre
places.fact: Millions of stars packed within a few light-years of Sgr A*, the magnetised threads of the Radio Arc, and the Central Molecular Zone, the densest gas in the galaxy.
places.type: the crowded core of the Milky Way
readout: star density here is a million times the Sun's neighbourhood
the night sky would hold thousands of stars brighter than Sirius

places.name: 3C 273
places.fact: A black hole of nearly a billion Suns feeding so fast its core outshines the whole galaxy 100 times. Its jet runs 200,000 light-years. Inner parts are drawn magnified, as the scale bar shows.
places.type: quasar · the first one ever identified (1963)
readout: 2.4 billion light-years · light left it before animals existed
jets at 0.90c: near jet boosted x58.6, far jet x0.29

places.name: SN 1987A
places.fact: In 1987 a blue supergiant's core collapsed in under a second. The flash lit up rings the star shed 20,000 years earlier; then the blast hit them. Replayed on a loop.
places.type: core-collapse supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud
readout: blue supergiant, ~20 solar masses
the rings are gas it shed ~20,000 years ago

places.name: Crab Nebula
places.fact: The wreck of a star seen exploding in 1054. A city-sized neutron star spinning 30 times a second at its heart powers the whole nebula.
places.type: supernova remnant and pulsar wind nebula · M1
readout: about 11 light-years across, expanding at 1,500 km/s
light from it takes 6,500 years to reach us

places.name: Crab Pulsar
places.fact: A ball of neutrons as dense as an atomic nucleus, spinning 30 times a second. Beams from its magnetic poles sweep past Earth like a lighthouse.
places.type: neutron star · 1.4 Suns crushed into 20 km
readout: P = 33.7 ms (shown ~50x slower) · slowing 38 ns per day
its spin-down powers the nebula: ~4.5x10^31 W

places.name: Whirlpool Galaxy
places.fact: The arms are a density wave that stars drift through, lighting up pink star-forming nebulae. The small galaxy NGC 5195 tugs on the end of one arm.
places.type: grand-design spiral with a companion · M51
readout: 31 million light-years · 76,000 light-years across
one lap of its disk takes ~200 million years (sped up here)

places.name: Antennae Galaxies
places.fact: Two spirals in the middle of a collision. Tides fling stars into long tails and colliding gas ignites bursts of star formation. Replayed here: 600 million years in a minute.
places.type: colliding galaxies · NGC 4038/4039
readout: nuclei 196,000 light-years apart
restricted N-body: 13,000 stars

places.name: Pillars of Creation
places.fact: Towers of cold gas and dust are eroded by ultraviolet light from the young cluster NGC 6611. Stars forming inside their tips fire jets out of the dust.
places.type: star-forming columns in the Eagle Nebula · M16
readout: the tallest pillar is ~4 light-years high
ultraviolet from O-type stars boils its surface away

places.name: Cat's Eye Nebula
places.fact: A dying Sun-like star puffed off a shell every ~1,500 years, leaving a bull's-eye of rings around twisted inner bubbles lit by its exposed hot core.
places.type: planetary nebula · NGC 6543 · what the Sun will become
readout: central star ~80,000 K, losing mass in a 1,900 km/s wind
teal: oxygen · red and orange: nitrogen and hydrogen

places.name: RS Ophiuchi
places.fact: A red giant overflows its Roche lobe and feeds a white dwarf. Every ~15 years the piled-up hydrogen ignites in a nova that blasts out an hourglass shell (last in 2021).
places.type: recurrent nova · red giant feeding a white dwarf
readout: orbital period ~454 days (shown ~20 s) · gas crossing L1

places.name: Saturn
places.fact: Its icy rings span 20 Earths yet are about 10 metres thick. Titan, bigger than Mercury, circles far outside them wrapped in orange haze.
places.type: gas giant · the ringed planet
readout: inside the rings: countless chunks of water ice
from dust grains to boulders the size of houses

places.name: Titan
places.fact: Bigger than Mercury and wrapped in a thick orange haze. Beneath it lie lakes and seas of liquid methane, rain and rivers: the only other world with standing liquid on its surface.
places.type: moon of Saturn
readout: thick nitrogen atmosphere, 1.5x Earth's surface pressure
lakes of liquid methane and ethane at -179 °C

places.name: Enceladus
places.fact: A small, brilliant ice moon whose south pole sprays geysers of salty water from an ocean below into space, feeding Saturn's E ring.
places.type: moon of Saturn
readout: radius 252 km · reflects 99% of sunlight
geysers of water vapour from its tiger stripes

places.name: Mimas
places.fact: A ball of ice 396 km across with one enormous crater, Herschel, 130 km wide: about a third of the moon's own width. Its walls rise about 5 km and a peak 6 km high stands in the middle, which is why Mimas looks like the Death Star from Star Wars.
places.type: moon of Saturn · the one with the giant crater
readout: 396 km across · Herschel is 130 km wide
Herschel is turned away from the Sun; it is lit for half of each orbit

places.name: Tethys
places.fact: A moon 1,062 km across made almost entirely of water ice: its density, 0.98 g/cm³, is just under water's. Ithaca Chasma, a canyon up to 100 km wide and about 3 km deep, runs some 2,000 km across it, and the crater Odysseus is 445 km wide, more than two fifths of the moon's width.
places.type: moon of Saturn · almost pure ice
readout: 1,062 km across · density 0.98 g/cm³, nearly pure ice
the dark band on the side it leads with comes from fast electrons in Saturn's magnetic field

places.name: Dione
places.fact: An icy moon 1,123 km across. Its darker trailing side is streaked with bright cliffs of ice, some of them hundreds of metres high, the walls of canyons where the dark surface material has fallen off; its gravity and shape suggest an ocean about 65 km deep under 100 km of ice.
places.type: moon of Saturn · with cliffs of bright ice
readout: 1,123 km across · density 1.48 g/cm³, ice and rock
its leading side is 1.6 times as bright as its trailing side

places.name: Rhea
places.fact: Saturn's second-largest moon, 1,527 km across, about three quarters ice and one quarter rock. In 2010 Cassini flew through a whisper of oxygen and carbon dioxide around it, the first oxygen atmosphere sampled directly at a world other than Earth.
places.type: moon of Saturn · the second-largest
readout: 1,527 km across · orbit 4.5 days, 527,000 km from Saturn
Inktomi: a young crater 47 km wide with rays hundreds of km long

places.name: GW170817
places.fact: Two neutron stars spiral in, shaking spacetime with gravitational waves, collide, collapse to a black hole and fling out a kilonova that forged gold. Replayed on a loop.
places.type: neutron star merger · first seen in gravitational waves and light
readout: f_gw = 146 Hz · separation 120 km
spacetime ripples at light speed

places.name: Alpha Centauri
places.fact: Two Sun-like stars circle each other every 80 years, 4.37 light-years away. The red dwarf Proxima, the closest star of all, orbits them far out.
places.type: nearest Sun-like star · a triple system
readout: A and B are 11 to 35 AU apart (like Saturn to Neptune)
from here our Sun is a bright star in Cassiopeia

places.name: Proxima Centauri
places.fact: A small, cool, flaring red dwarf 4.25 light-years away. Its planet Proxima b orbits in 11 days inside the zone where water could be liquid.
places.type: red dwarf · the closest star to the Sun
readout: 15% of the Sun's width, 0.2% of its light
frequent flares brighten it many times over

places.name: Proxima b
places.fact: An Earth-mass planet 7.5 million km from its star, closer than Mercury is to the Sun, yet only warm because Proxima is so dim.
places.type: exoplanet · rocky, probably tidally locked
readout: orbit 11.2 days · 0.049 AU from Proxima
tidally locked: one hemisphere always faces its star

places.name: Sirius
places.fact: Twice the Sun's mass and 25 times as bright. Its faint partner Sirius B is a white dwarf: a Sun's worth of matter squeezed into a ball the size of Earth.
places.type: brightest star in the night sky · with a white dwarf companion
readout: 8.6 light-years · 25 times the Sun's luminosity
Sirius B: 12,000 km across, 1 solar mass

places.name: Sirius B
places.fact: The exposed core of a dead star, about the size of Earth but as massive as the Sun. A teaspoon of it would weigh several tonnes.
places.type: white dwarf
readout: surface 25,000 K · slowly cooling for billions of years

places.name: Vega
places.fact: Spins so fast (once every 12.5 hours) it bulges at the equator and has a hot pole and a cooler waist. We happen to look straight down on its pole.
places.type: fast-spinning A star seen pole-on
readout: 25 light-years · was the pole star 14,000 years ago

places.name: Polaris
places.fact: A Cepheid supergiant that breathes in and out every 4 days. Earth's axis happens to point almost straight at it, so the whole northern sky turns around it.
places.type: the North Star · a pulsating supergiant
readout: 433 light-years · 1,260 times the Sun's luminosity

places.name: Rigel
places.fact: A blue-white supergiant about 120,000 times as luminous as the Sun. It is burning through its fuel so fast it will explode within a few million years.
places.type: blue supergiant in Orion
readout: 860 light-years · 79 times the Sun's radius

places.name: Antares
places.fact: So large that, placed where the Sun is, its surface would reach beyond the orbit of Mars. A hot blue companion orbits in its dusty wind.
places.type: red supergiant · the heart of the Scorpion
readout: 680 times the Sun's radius (3.2 AU) · 550 light-years
it will end as a supernova, maybe within 100,000 years

places.name: Deneb
places.fact: About 200,000 times as luminous as the Sun. From 2,600 light-years away it still shines as the tail of the Swan.
places.type: white supergiant · one of the most luminous stars we can see
readout: ~2,600 light-years (uncertain) · 203 solar radii

places.name: Arcturus
places.fact: An old star that has run out of hydrogen in its core and swollen to 25 times the Sun's width: a preview of the Sun in about 5 billion years.
places.type: orange giant · brightest star of the northern sky
readout: 36.7 light-years · moving fast through the Milky Way's disk

places.name: Canopus
places.fact: The second-brightest star in the night sky, a white giant 73 times the Sun's width and about 16,600 times as luminous. Since Mariner 4 in 1964, spacecraft have steered by it to keep themselves pointed the right way.
places.type: white bright giant · second-brightest star in the night sky
readout: 310 light-years · 73 times the Sun's radius
about 16,600 times as luminous as the Sun, 7,660 K

places.name: Aldebaran
places.fact: An orange giant 44 times wider than the Sun. Pioneer 10 is heading its way and will pass it in about 2 million years.
places.type: orange giant · the eye of the Bull
readout: 65 light-years · 44 solar radii

places.name: Barnard's Star
places.fact: An ancient red dwarf racing across the sky, the second-closest star system to the Sun. Four small planets were found around it in 2024-25.
places.type: red dwarf · fastest-moving star in our sky
readout: 5.96 light-years · about 10 billion years old

places.name: Tau Ceti
places.fact: A Sun-like star 11.9 light-years away, older than the Sun and poorer in metals. In 1960 it was one of the first two stars searched for alien radio signals, and four planets a few times Earth's mass may orbit it.
places.type: nearby Sun-like star
readout: 11.9 light-years · 79% of the Sun's width, 5,320 K
4 candidate planets, each at least 1.7 Earth masses

places.name: Epsilon Eridani
places.fact: A young, active star about 500 million years old, ringed by belts of icy debris like a young Solar System.
places.type: young Sun-like star with debris belts
readout: 10.5 light-years · outer debris ring ~65 AU from the star

places.name: Capella
places.fact: Two giant stars, each about 2.5 times the Sun's mass, circling each other every 104 days, 0.74 AU apart. The cooler one, 12 times the Sun's width, is near the end of burning helium in its core; the hotter, 9 times the Sun's width, has left the main sequence and is still swelling toward the red giant stage.
places.type: yellow giants · a pair circling every 104 days
readout: 42.9 light-years · two giants 0.74 AU apart, 4,970 K and 5,730 K
sped up here: one lap in 30 s, really 104 days

places.name: Altair
places.fact: Spins once every 9 hours, so fast it is squashed 20% flatter at the poles. Interferometers have imaged its bright poles and dim equator.
places.type: rapidly rotating A star
readout: 16.7 light-years · equator spins at 286 km/s

places.name: Spica
places.fact: Two hot blue stars 0.13 AU apart, closer than Mercury is to the Sun, circling each other every four days. The bigger one, 11 times the Sun's mass, spins fast enough to bulge about 6% at its equator, and its partner's pull stretches it a few per cent more; it will probably end as a supernova.
places.type: hot blue stars · a pair circling every four days
readout: 250 light-years · 25,300 K and 20,900 K
sped up here: one lap in 8 s, really 4.01 days

places.name: TRAPPIST-1
places.fact: A star barely larger than Jupiter with seven rocky planets packed inside an orbit smaller than Mercury's. Three sit where liquid water is possible.
places.type: ultracool dwarf with seven Earth-sized planets
readout: all seven planets fit within 0.062 AU of the star
from one planet, the others look bigger than our Moon

places.name: TRAPPIST-1e
places.fact: The most Earth-like of the seven: about Earth's size and density, in the zone where water could stay liquid. It probably keeps one side facing its star, as the Moon does with Earth.
places.type: exoplanet
readout: orbit 6.1 days at 0.02925 AU · 0.92 times Earth's width
illustrative: the sea under its star and the ice around it are a guess; no one knows yet if it has air or water

places.name: Betelgeuse
places.fact: Placed where the Sun is, it would swallow Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. Its surface is a few giant boiling cells; in 2019-20 it dimmed when it coughed out a cloud of dust. It will explode as a supernova.
places.type: red supergiant · the shoulder of Orion
readout: 764 times the Sun's radius · 3.6 AU · 548 light-years
about 100,000 times as luminous as the Sun, and only ~10 million years old

places.name: Eta Carinae
places.fact: In the 1840s this star blew off ten Suns' worth of gas and briefly became the second-brightest star in the sky. That debris is the Homunculus. It may explode as a supernova or hypernova.
places.type: hypergiant binary inside the Homunculus Nebula
readout: two stars of ~90 and ~30 solar masses on a 5.5-year orbit
their colliding winds glow in X-rays at 3,000 km/s

places.name: SGR 1806-20
places.fact: A neutron star with a magnetic field a thousand trillion times Earth's. On 27 December 2004 its crust cracked and released more energy in 0.2 s than the Sun does in 250,000 years. Replayed on a loop.
places.type: magnetar · the strongest magnetic field known
readout: field ~10^15 gauss: it would wipe credit cards from halfway to the Moon
stress building in the twisted field

places.name: Omega Centauri
places.fact: Ten million stars packed into a ball 150 light-years across, possibly the stripped core of a small galaxy the Milky Way swallowed. Fast stars at its centre betray a black hole of ~8,000 Suns.
places.type: globular cluster · 10 million stars
readout: 17,000 light-years · 12 billion years old
near the centre, stars are 0.1 light-years apart; its night sky would blaze

places.name: Andromeda Galaxy
places.fact: A trillion stars 2.5 million light-years away, the most distant thing most people can see without a telescope. It is falling toward us at 110 km/s and will merge with the Milky Way in about 4.5 billion years.
places.type: giant spiral · our nearest big neighbour · M31
readout: 2.5 million light-years: you see it as it was when our ancestors first made stone tools
~220,000 light-years across, about twice the Milky Way

places.name: M32
places.fact: A small, dense galaxy close to Andromeda, and the first galaxy of the elliptical kind ever recorded: Guillaume Le Gentil saw it in 1749, long before anyone knew what galaxies were. It may be the stripped core of a big galaxy that Andromeda swallowed about 2 billion years ago.
places.type: compact elliptical galaxy · satellite of Andromeda
readout: 2.52 million light-years · about 6,400 light-years across
its black hole weighs about 2.5 million Suns

places.name: M110
places.fact: A dwarf elliptical galaxy that orbits Andromeda. Messier saw it in 1773 and included it in his drawing of Andromeda but never listed it; Caroline Herschel found it on her own in 1783, and it was given the number 110 only in 1967. Unlike most of its kind it holds dust and young stars near its centre.
places.type: dwarf elliptical galaxy · satellite of Andromeda
readout: 2.73 million light-years · about 17,000 light-years across
about 130,000 to 190,000 light-years behind Andromeda

places.name: M87
places.fact: One of the most massive galaxies nearby, swarming with some 12,000 globular clusters. From its core a jet of plasma shoots out at nearly the speed of light.
places.type: giant elliptical galaxy at the heart of the Virgo Cluster
readout: 53.5 million light-years · about 2.4 trillion solar masses
its black hole weighs 6.5 billion Suns

places.name: the M87 jet
places.fact: Electrons spiral in magnetic fields at 99% of the speed of light. Blobs in the jet appear to move up to six times faster than light, an illusion caused by their speed toward us.
places.type: relativistic jet · 5,000 light-years long
readout: apparent speed up to 6c: the blobs almost keep pace with their own light
beamed toward us, so the far-side counter-jet is invisible

places.name: M87*
places.fact: Its event horizon is wider than our entire Solar System: Neptune's orbit would fit inside it 60 times over. The Event Horizon Telescope photographed its glowing ring in 2019.
places.type: supermassive black hole · 6.5 billion Suns · first ever imaged (2019)
readout: event horizon 38 billion km across (256 AU)
light takes a day and a half to cross it

places.name: HL Tauri
places.fact: A star less than a million years old. Its disk of dust is already carved into rings and gaps, probably by young planets sweeping up material. Colours show the dust glow ALMA sees.
places.type: newborn star and planet-forming disk
readout: disk ~240 AU across · gaps at 13, 32, 42, 50, 64, 74, 81 AU
450 light-years away in Taurus

places.name: TON 618
places.fact: A black hole of about 40 billion Suns powering a quasar 140 trillion times brighter than the Sun. Its event horizon would swallow the Solar System out to 50 times Neptune's distance.
places.type: hyperluminous quasar · one of the most massive black holes known
places.where: light left it 10.8 billion years ago · now ~18 billion light-years away
readout: event horizon ~1,600 AU across; light takes 9 days to cross it
we see it as it was 10.8 billion years ago

places.name: Bullet Cluster
places.fact: Two clusters collided at 4,500 km/s. Their galaxies and invisible dark matter (blue, mapped by gravitational lensing) sailed through; their hot gas (pink, seen in X-rays) crashed and lagged behind.
places.type: colliding galaxy clusters · dark matter made visible
readout: the strongest direct evidence that dark matter is real
its gas is 100 million °C

places.name: JADES-GS-z14-0
places.fact: Seen by JWST as it was just 290 million years after the Big Bang. Already bright and surprisingly large, it is one of the most distant galaxies ever confirmed.
places.type: one of the most distant galaxies ever confirmed
places.where: light left it 13.5 billion years ago · now ~33 billion light-years away
readout: redshift 14.3: its light is stretched 15 times
from ultraviolet into the infrared by the expanding universe

places.name: Voyager 1
places.fact: Launched in 1977, it flew past Jupiter and Saturn and in 2012 became the first craft to enter interstellar space. Its radio signal, 20 watts, takes about a day to reach us.
places.type: space probe · the farthest human-made object
readout: moving at 17 km/s · light-time to Earth 23 h 58 min
one light-day from Earth on 18 November 2026
from here the Sun is only the brightest star; Earth is invisible

places.name: Voyager 2
places.fact: Voyager 1's twin took the grand tour past all four giant planets and crossed into interstellar space in 2018, heading south below the plane of the planets.
places.type: space probe · the only visitor to Uranus and Neptune
readout: 144 AU out · 15 km/s

places.name: New Horizons
places.fact: Flew past Pluto in 2015 and the icy Kuiper-belt object Arrokoth in 2019, and is still heading out of the Solar System.
places.type: space probe · first to Pluto
readout: 65 AU out · 14 km/s · the size of a grand piano, powered by plutonium

places.name: James Webb Space Telescope
places.fact: Parked 1.5 million km from Earth, always in Earth's shadow side, behind a sunshield the size of a tennis court. Its 6.5 m gold mirror sees the first galaxies.
places.type: infrared space telescope at Sun-Earth L2
readout: sunshield 21 x 14 m keeps the telescope at -233 °C
it has seen galaxies from 290 million years after the Big Bang

places.name: International Space Station
places.fact: The largest thing humans have built in space: a football pitch of solar wings and modules, lived in continuously since November 2000. It circles Earth every 93 minutes at 28,000 km/h.
places.type: crewed space station · 420 km up, 16 orbits a day
readout: orbit 51.6° to the equator · 16 sunrises a day

places.name: Hubble Space Telescope
places.fact: A school-bus-sized telescope above the blur of the atmosphere. In 35 years it has measured the expansion of the universe and looked back to galaxies 13 billion years old.
places.type: space telescope · 530 km up since 1990
readout: 2.4 m mirror · one orbit every 95 minutes

places.name: Mount Everest and the Himalaya
places.fact: Mount Everest, on the border of Nepal and China, is the highest mountain above sea level: 8,849 m. Nepal and China agreed that height in 2020.
places.type: mountains on the border of Nepal and China
readout: summit 8,849 m above sea level · 27.99° N, 86.92° E

places.name: Grand Canyon
places.fact: The Grand Canyon in Arizona is 446 km long, up to 29 km wide and up to about 1,800 m deep. The Colorado River cut it through the rock.
places.type: a canyon in Arizona, United States
readout: 446 km long, up to 1,800 m deep · 36.09° N, 112.11° W

places.name: The Alps: Matterhorn and Mont Blanc
places.fact: Mont Blanc, about 4,806 m high, is the highest peak in the Alps; its snowy top rises and falls by a few metres from year to year. The Matterhorn, 4,478 m, stands on the border of Switzerland and Italy.
places.type: mountains in France, Italy and Switzerland
readout: Mont Blanc about 4,806 m, Matterhorn 4,478 m · 45.90° N, 7.26° E

places.name: Mount Kilimanjaro
places.fact: Kilimanjaro in Tanzania is Africa's highest mountain: 5,895 m above sea level. It is a volcano that stands alone, just over 3 degrees south of the equator, with ice on its summit.
places.type: a volcano in Tanzania
readout: Uhuru Peak 5,895 m · 3.08° S, 37.35° E

places.name: Mount Fuji
places.fact: Mount Fuji is Japan's highest mountain, a volcano 3,776 m high. It last erupted in 1707.
places.type: a volcano in Japan

places.name: Yosemite Valley
places.fact: El Capitan, in Yosemite Valley, California, is a granite wall that rises about 900 m from the valley floor to its top. Half Dome rises at the other end of the valley.
places.type: a valley in California, United States
readout: El Capitan rises 900 m · 37.74° N, 119.58° W

places.name: Torres del Paine
places.fact: Torres del Paine National Park is in Chilean Patagonia. Torres means towers in Spanish, and paine means blue in the Tehuelche language.
places.type: a national park in Chile
readout: UNESCO biosphere reserve since 1978 · 50.95° S, 73.00° W

places.name: Denali
places.fact: Denali, in Alaska, is the highest mountain in North America: 6,190 m above sea level. Its name comes from a Koyukon word for high, and since 2025 the US government calls it Mount McKinley.
places.type: a mountain in Alaska, United States

places.name: Richat Structure, Sahara
places.fact: The Richat Structure in Mauritania is a ring of eroded rock about 40 km across. Early space crews used it as a landmark.
places.type: a ring of rock in Mauritania
readout: about 40 km across · 21.12° N, 11.40° W

places.name: Meeting of Waters, Amazon
places.fact: Near Manaus in Brazil, the dark Rio Negro meets the pale Solimoes, and below them the river is called the Amazon. The two waters flow side by side with a sharp line between them and take about 100 km to mix fully.
places.type: rivers in Brazil
readout: about 100 km to mix fully · 3.14° S, 59.92° W

places.name: Nile Delta
places.fact: The Nile Delta in Egypt fans out to about 240 km of Mediterranean coast. It is green farmland in a desert.
places.type: a river delta in Egypt
readout: about 240 km of coast · 30.90° N, 31.15° E

places.name: Uluru and Kata Tjuta
places.fact: Uluru, in Australia's Northern Territory, rises 348 m above the plain and is 863 m above sea level. Much of the rock lies underground.
places.type: a sandstone rock in Australia
readout: 348 m above the plain · 25.34° S, 131.04° E

places.name: Okavango Delta
places.fact: The Okavango Delta in Botswana is where a river ends in the Kalahari sand, not the sea. In flood, its water spreads over as much as 15,000 km².
places.type: an inland delta in Botswana
readout: floods up to 15,000 km² · 19.30° S, 22.80° E

places.name: Sossusvlei dunes, Namib
places.fact: Sossusvlei, in the Namib Desert of Namibia, is a clay pan among red dunes. The dune called Big Daddy is about 325 m high.
places.type: dunes in Namibia
readout: dunes up to about 325 m · 24.74° S, 15.30° E

places.name: Great Barrier Reef: Whitsundays and Heart Reef
places.fact: The Great Barrier Reef off Queensland is made of more than 2,900 reefs and 900 islands along 2,300 km. It is the largest coral reef system on Earth.
places.type: a coral reef in Australia

places.name: Hawaii: the Big Island and Kilauea
places.fact: Kilauea, on the Big Island of Hawaii, is one of the most active volcanoes on Earth. Mauna Kea, on the same island, rises 4,207 m above sea level.
places.type: a volcanic island in Hawaii, United States
readout: Kilauea 1,247 m, Mauna Kea 4,207 m · 19.41° N, 155.28° W

places.name: Iceland: Vatnajokull and Jokulsarlon
places.fact: Vatnajokull is the biggest ice cap in Iceland. On its southern edge, the volcano Oraefajokull holds the highest point in the country, Hvannadalshnukur: 2,110 m.
places.type: an ice cap in Iceland
readout: Hvannadalshnukur 2,110 m · 64.05° N, 16.55° W

places.name: Antarctica: Ross Island and the Ross Ice Shelf
places.fact: The Ross Ice Shelf is the largest floating ice shelf in Antarctica, about 500,000 km². Mount Erebus, on Ross Island at its edge, is the southernmost active volcano on Earth: 3,794 m.
places.type: an island and an ice shelf in Antarctica
readout: Ross Ice Shelf about 500,000 km² · 77.53° S, 167.17° E

places.name: Greenland: Ilulissat Icefjord
places.fact: Sermeq Kujalleq feeds the Ilulissat Icefjord in Greenland. It is one of the fastest glaciers on Earth: in 2012 it moved up to 46 m a day.
places.type: a glacier and its fjord in Greenland
readout: up to 46 m a day · 69.17° N, 50.55° W

places.name: The Maldives
places.fact: The Maldives are a chain of 26 coral atolls in the Indian Ocean. It is the lowest country on Earth: the ground is about 1.5 m above sea level on average.
places.type: coral atolls in the Indian Ocean
readout: ground 1.5 m above the sea on average · 4.20° N, 73.50° E

places.name: Bora Bora
places.fact: Bora Bora, in French Polynesia, is what is left of an extinct volcano, ringed by a lagoon and a reef. Its peak, Mount Otemanu, is 727 m high.
places.type: an island in French Polynesia
readout: Mount Otemanu 727 m · 16.50° S, 151.74° W

places.name: Ha Long Bay
places.fact: Ha Long Bay in Vietnam has about 1,600 limestone islands and islets rising from the sea. UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site in 1994.
places.type: a bay in Vietnam
readout: about 1,600 islands · 20.85° N, 107.10° E

places.name: Geirangerfjord
places.fact: Geirangerfjord in Norway is a narrow fjord about 15 km long, with waterfalls dropping straight into it. UNESCO listed it in 2005.
places.type: a fjord in Norway
readout: fjord about 15 km long · 62.10° N, 7.15° E

places.name: Palm Jumeirah, Dubai
places.fact: Palm Jumeirah in Dubai is an island built from sea sand and mountain rock, begun in 2001. From above it is a palm tree with 17 fronds.
places.type: an island built in the sea, Dubai
readout: 17 fronds, built from the sea · 25.11° N, 55.14° E

places.name: Panama Canal
places.fact: The Panama Canal is about 82 km long. Locks lift ships 26 m up to Gatun Lake and lower them again on the other side.
places.type: a canal in Panama
readout: about 82 km long, Gatun Lake 26 m up · 9.12° N, 79.70° W

places.name: Great Wall at Mutianyu
places.fact: All the walls and trenches of the Great Wall of China, from every dynasty, add up to 21,196 km (China's 2012 survey). Mutianyu is a restored stretch northeast of Beijing.
places.type: a wall in China

places.name: Pyramids of Giza
places.fact: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built about 4,500 years ago. It was 146.6 m high when new and is 138.5 m high now.
places.type: pyramids in Egypt
readout: 138.5 m high, 230 m wide at the base · 29.98° N, 31.13° E

places.name: Suez Canal
places.fact: The Suez Canal in Egypt joins the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. It opened in 1869 and is now 193 km long.
places.type: a canal in Egypt

places.name: Three Gorges Dam
places.fact: The Three Gorges Dam on China's Yangtze River is 2,335 m long and 181 m high. Its power station is the biggest in the world, at 22,500 MW.
places.type: a dam in China

places.name: Hoover Dam and Lake Mead
places.fact: Hoover Dam, on the border of Nevada and Arizona, is 221 m high. Lake Mead behind it is the biggest reservoir in the United States by capacity.
places.type: a dam in the United States
readout: dam 221 m high, 379 m long · 36.02° N, 114.74° W

places.name: Tranquility Base
places.fact: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed here in the lunar module Eagle on 20 July 1969, the first people to walk on another world. They spent about two and a half hours outside; Eagle's descent stage still stands where they left it.
places.type: Apollo 11 landing site on the Moon
readout: 0.67° N, 23.47° E · landed 20 July 1969 · 2 h 31 min outside · 21.5 kg of rock and soil brought home

places.name: Apollo 12 landing site
places.fact: Pete Conrad and Alan Bean landed the lunar module Intrepid here on 19 November 1969, about 160 m from Surveyor 3, a robot lander that had touched down in April 1967. They walked to it and brought pieces of it home.
places.type: in the Ocean of Storms, on the Moon
readout: 3.01° S, 23.42° W · landed 19 November 1969 · 7 h 45 min outside in two walks · 34.3 kg of rock and soil brought home

places.name: Apollo 14 landing site
places.fact: Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell landed Antares here in the Fra Mauro hills on 5 February 1971 and climbed toward the rim of Cone crater, about 340 m wide, pulling their tools on a cart. Before leaving, Shepard hit two golf balls.
places.type: at Fra Mauro, on the Moon
readout: 3.65° S, 17.47° W · landed 5 February 1971 · 9 h 22 min outside in two walks · 42.3 kg of rock and soil brought home

places.name: Apollo 15 landing site
places.fact: David Scott and James Irwin landed Falcon here on 30 July 1971, between the Apennine mountains and Hadley Rille, and drove the first lunar rover. Among the 77 kg of rock they brought home is the Genesis Rock, a piece of the Moon's early crust.
places.type: at Hadley-Apennine, on the Moon
readout: 26.13° N, 3.63° E · landed 30 July 1971 · 18 h 35 min outside in three drives · 27.9 km driven

places.name: Hadley Rille
places.fact: A winding channel 116 km long, about 1.2 km wide and up to about 300 m deep, probably cut by flowing lava more than 3 billion years ago. Apollo 15's crew drove to its edge and sampled the layers of rock in its wall.
places.type: a lava channel on the Moon
readout: 26.11° N, 3.55° E · 116 km long · about 1.2 km wide · about 300 m deep by the Apollo 15 site

places.name: Apollo 16 landing site
places.fact: John Young and Charles Duke landed Orion here on 21 April 1972 (UTC), the only landing in the Moon's central highlands. They expected volcanic rock and found mostly breccias, rocks smashed and welded together by impacts.
places.type: at Descartes, on the Moon
readout: 8.97° S, 15.50° E · landed 21 April 1972 (UTC) · 20 h 14 min outside in three drives · 95.7 kg of rock and soil brought home

places.name: Apollo 17 landing site
places.fact: Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt, a geologist, landed Challenger in the valley of Taurus-Littrow on 11 December 1972, the last people to walk on the Moon so far. At Shorty crater they found orange soil, beads of volcanic glass.
places.type: in the valley of Taurus-Littrow, on the Moon
readout: 20.19° N, 30.77° E · landed 11 December 1972 · 22 h 4 min outside in three drives · 110.5 kg of rock and soil brought home

places.name: Tycho
places.fact: One of the youngest big craters on the Moon's near side, 85 km wide and 4.8 km deep, thought to be about 108 million years old. Its bright rays reach across much of the near side. Surveyor 7 landed in 1968 on the rock it threw out, about 28 km north of its rim.
places.type: a young crater on the Moon
readout: 43.31° S, 11.36° W · 85 km wide · 4.8 km deep · central peak about 2 km high · about 108 million years old

places.name: Copernicus
places.fact: A crater 96 km wide and about 800 million years old, with terraced walls and a cluster of mountains in the middle. Its age comes from glass in Apollo 12's soil thought to have been thrown out by the impact.
places.type: a crater on the Moon
readout: 9.62° N, 20.08° W · 96 km wide · 3.8 km deep · central peaks up to about 1.2 km high · about 800 million years old

places.name: Orion Nebula
places.fact: The nearest big star factory, visible to the naked eye as the fuzzy middle "star" of Orion's sword. Four hot young stars at its heart, the Trapezium, light the whole cloud.
places.type: stellar nursery · M42 · in the sword of Orion
readout: 1,344 light-years · about 24 light-years across
~2,000 newborn stars, most under a million years old

places.name: Horsehead Nebula
places.fact: A pillar of cold, dusty gas that happens to look like a horse's head, silhouetted against glowing hydrogen lit by the star sigma Orionis.
places.type: dark nebula · Barnard 33 · in Orion
readout: 1,375 light-years · the head is about 3.5 light-years tall
it is slowly being eroded and will be gone in ~5 million years

places.name: Helix Nebula
places.fact: One of the closest planetary nebulae: the outer layers of a dying Sun-like star, blown into a double ring that looks like a giant eye. Its inner edge is peppered with thousands of comet-shaped knots.
places.type: planetary nebula · NGC 7293 · "the Eye of God"
readout: 655 light-years · 2.9 light-years across
its central white dwarf is about 100,000 °C

places.name: Ring Nebula
places.fact: A glowing barrel of gas thrown off by a dying star, seen almost end-on so it looks like a smoke ring. The blue-green centre is oxygen; the red rim is hydrogen and nitrogen.
places.type: planetary nebula · M57 · in Lyra
readout: 2,570 light-years · about a light-year across
seen from the side it is a hollow barrel, not a ring

places.name: Carina Nebula
places.fact: Four times bigger than the Orion Nebula and home to some of the most massive stars known, including Eta Carinae. Its dust pillars, like Mystic Mountain, are being carved by their light.
places.type: giant star-forming region · NGC 3372
readout: ~7,500 light-years · about 300 light-years across
its clusters hold dozens of stars over 50 times the Sun's mass

places.name: Veil Nebula
places.fact: The expanding wreckage of a star that exploded 10,000 to 20,000 years ago. The blast wave is still ploughing into surrounding gas, lighting it up in long twisted filaments.
places.type: supernova remnant · the Cygnus Loop
readout: 2,400 light-years · about 110 light-years across
the shock is still racing outward at ~1.5 million km/h

places.name: Eagle Nebula
places.fact: A cavity 20 light-years wide, blown into a cold cloud by the hot young stars of NGC 6611. What is left of the cloud stands in columns pointing back at the cluster: the Pillars of Creation, the 9-light-year Spire and a dozen smaller trunks.
places.type: star-forming region · M16, home of the Pillars of Creation
readout: 6,500 light-years · about 70 x 55 light-years
the Pillars are about 10 light-years from the cluster that is slowly destroying them

places.name: Sculptor Galaxy
places.fact: One of the brightest galaxies in our sky and one of the dustiest. Its core is forming stars so fast that the explosions drive a wind of gas out of the galaxy.
places.type: dusty starburst spiral · NGC 253
readout: 11.4 million light-years · about 90,000 light-years across
its starburst core makes stars dozens of times faster than the Milky Way

places.name: Cartwheel Galaxy
places.fact: A smaller galaxy punched straight through this one a few hundred million years ago. The collision sent a ripple outward like a stone dropped in a pond, and the expanding ring is lit up with new stars.
places.type: ring galaxy · ESO 350-40
readout: 500 million light-years · 150,000 light-years across
the collision happened a few hundred million years ago

places.name: Hoag's Object
places.fact: A nearly perfect ring of young blue stars around a ball of old yellow ones, with an empty gap between them. Nobody is sure how it formed. Through the gap you can see another, far more distant ring galaxy.
places.type: ring galaxy · a perfect ring around a yellow core
readout: 612 million light-years · the ring is about 120,000 light-years across
its core is only 17,000 light-years wide

places.name: Stephan's Quintet
places.fact: Four galaxies caught in a slow-motion pile-up 290 million light-years away. One of them is ramming through the group so fast it has lit a shock wave bigger than the Milky Way. The fifth galaxy is a foreground impostor.
places.type: compact galaxy group · four colliding galaxies (and one impostor)
readout: 290 million light-years · the shock front is about 100,000 light-years long
the lone blue galaxy NGC 7320 is only 40 million light-years away

places.name: NGC 1275
places.fact: A monster galaxy at the centre of the Perseus Cluster. Its black hole blows bubbles in the surrounding hot gas, and long red filaments of cooling gas, some wider than the Milky Way, hang around it like seaweed.
places.type: giant galaxy at the heart of the Perseus Cluster · Perseus A
readout: 237 million light-years · filaments up to 200,000 light-years long
the black hole in its core sings the lowest note known: a B flat 57 octaves below middle C

places.name: UY Scuti
places.fact: Placed where the Sun is, its surface would reach most of the way to Jupiter. If it were a hollow ball, hundreds of millions of Suns would fit inside. Even so it is only 7 to 10 times the Sun's mass: it is enormous but thin.
places.type: red supergiant · one of the largest stars known
readout: 909 times the Sun's radius (8.5 AU across) · 5,900 light-years
light takes about 70 minutes to cross it

places.name: Stephenson 2-18
places.fact: If its measured size is right, its surface would reach beyond the orbit of Saturn. Its distance is uncertain by more than half, so it may be smaller, but it is certainly one of the giants of the galaxy.
places.type: red supergiant · possibly the largest star known
readout: ~2,150 times the Sun's radius (20 AU across) · ~19,000 light-years
light would take almost 3 hours to cross it

places.name: Tarantula Nebula
places.fact: A star factory in the Large Magellanic Cloud so bright that, if it were as close as the Orion Nebula, it would cast shadows on Earth. Its central cluster R136 holds the heaviest stars known.
places.type: the most active star-forming region in the Local Group · 30 Doradus
readout: 163,000 light-years, in the Large Magellanic Cloud · ~650 light-years across
supernova 1987A went off at its edge

places.name: R136a1
places.fact: Between 200 and 300 times the mass of the Sun and about 7 million times as bright. Stars this heavy blow themselves apart with winds of thousands of km/s and live only a few million years.
places.type: Wolf-Rayet star · the heaviest star known
readout: ~46,000 K surface · 43 times the Sun's radius
its wind carries off an Earth's mass every few months

places.name: WR 140
places.fact: A Wolf-Rayet star and an O-type giant on an 8-year orbit. Each time they swing close, their colliding winds squeeze out a puff of carbon soot. The James Webb telescope saw 17 of these shells nested like ripples.
places.type: colliding-wind binary · a dust-making machine
readout: 5,600 light-years · shells spaced about 0.07 light-years apart
the dust streams out at ~2,600 km/s

places.name: Gaia BH1
places.fact: The closest black hole we know of, 1,560 light-years away. It is not feeding, so it gives off no light at all: astronomers found it in 2022 from the wobble of the Sun-like star that circles it every 186 days. Look through it at that star and its light bends into arcs around the shadow.
places.type: the nearest known black hole · dormant · 9.6 Suns
readout: event horizon 57 km across, smaller than a city
its companion orbits 1.4 AU away, about the distance of Mars from the Sun

places.name: Cygnus X-1
places.fact: The first object widely accepted as a black hole (1971). Every 5.6 days it circles a blue supergiant 40 times the Sun's mass, stripping gas into a disk hot enough to shine in X-rays. Stephen Hawking famously bet it was not a black hole, and lost.
places.type: black hole feeding on a blue supergiant · 21 Suns
readout: the two orbit 0.2 AU apart, half of Mercury's distance from the Sun
X-rays come from gas at millions of degrees just before it falls in

places.name: A star torn apart
places.fact: When a star wanders too close to a giant black hole, the difference in gravity across it pulls it into a long stream of gas: "spaghettification". Half the debris is flung away; the rest falls back, forms a disk and flares for months. This one is modelled on AT2019qiz, the closest such flare yet seen.
places.type: tidal disruption event · modelled on AT2019qiz
readout: a Sun-like star falls toward a black hole of a million Suns
at 45 Schwarzschild radii its own gravity can no longer hold it together

places.name: GW150914
places.fact: 1.3 billion years ago two black holes of 36 and 29 Suns spiralled together and merged. They gave off no light, but three Suns' worth of energy left as ripples in spacetime, which reached detectors on Earth on 14 September 2015.
places.type: two black holes merging · the first gravitational waves detected
readout: wave frequency 35 Hz and rising: the "chirp"
the pair is circling 18 times a second (shown slowed down)

places.name: 'Oumuamua
places.fact: A reddish object a few hundred metres long (its size and shape are uncertain) that came from another star, swung past the Sun and is leaving forever at 26 km/s. It tumbled end over end and sped up slightly, as a comet would, without showing any tail.
places.type: the first interstellar object · passed the Sun in 2017
readout: 55 AU from the Sun and leaving at ~26 km/s
drawn as a long thin body, one of the shapes that fit its light curve

places.name: Arrokoth
places.fact: Two flattened lumps of ice that drifted together gently 4.5 billion years ago and stuck. New Horizons flew past it in 2019, 6.6 billion km from home: the most distant world any spacecraft has visited.
places.type: contact binary in the Kuiper belt · the farthest world ever visited
readout: 43.2 AU from the Sun · 36 km long
its two lobes are called Wenu and Weeyo

places.name: Halley's Comet
places.fact: A dirty snowball about 15 km long on a 76-year orbit. Near the Sun it grows a glowing coma and two tails: curved dust and straight blue gas, pushed away from the Sun. It was last close in 1986 and returns in 2061.
places.type: periodic comet · returns every 76 years
readout: 34.9 AU from the Sun: frozen, dark and tailless out here
it comes back in 2061 (set the time machine to see its tails)

places.name: Ceres
places.fact: A round world 940 km across holding a quarter of the asteroid belt's mass. NASA's Dawn found bright patches of salt in Occator crater, left by briny water welling up from below.
places.type: dwarf planet · the largest body in the asteroid belt
readout: 940 km across · 2.8 AU from the Sun
one day lasts 9 hours; a year, 4.6 of ours

places.name: Kepler-16b
places.fact: The first planet seen passing in front of two stars at once (2011). From its cloud tops there would be double sunrises and double sunsets. It is a cold gas giant, not a desert world.
places.type: circumbinary planet · a real world with two suns
readout: Saturn-sized · orbits both stars every 229 days (sped up here)
its two suns rise and set together

places.name: 55 Cancri
places.fact: A yellow dwarf a little smaller than the Sun with five known planets, one of them a lava world skimming its surface.
places.type: Sun-like star with five planets
readout: 41 light-years · visible to the eye from a dark site

places.name: 55 Cancri e
places.fact: Almost twice Earth's width and eight times its mass, so close to its star that its surface is probably molten rock. JWST measured its day side at about 1,500 °C, cooler than bare rock would be, a hint of a thick atmosphere perhaps breathed out by the magma.
places.type: lava world · a year of 18 hours
readout: orbit 17.7 hours (sped up here) at 0.015 AU
day side ~1,500 °C: hot enough to melt rock

places.name: KELT-9
places.fact: A hot, fast-spinning A0 star twice the Sun's size, with a giant planet roasting in a polar orbit around it.
places.type: hot blue-white star
readout: 670 light-years · 10,170 K

places.name: KELT-9b
places.fact: A gas giant puffed up to nearly twice Jupiter's width, with a day side around 4,300 °C: hotter than most stars. Its molecules are torn apart and its atmosphere is boiling off into space.
places.type: the hottest planet known
readout: orbit 1.5 days (sped up here) · day side ~4,300 °C
tidally locked: one side always faces the star

places.name: HR 8799
places.fact: One of the first planetary systems ever photographed directly (2008). Four giant planets, each several times Jupiter's mass, glow in infrared from the heat of their birth, some 30 to 40 million years ago.
places.type: young star with four photographed giant planets
readout: 133 light-years · planets 16 to 68 AU out (Jupiter's orbit is 5 AU)
orbits of about 50 to 460 years, sped up here

places.name: HR 8799 b
places.fact: A young giant planet still glowing from its formation, about 1,000 K at its cloud tops.
places.type: young giant planet · photographed directly
readout: 68 AU from its star · ~458 years per orbit

places.name: Cassiopeia A
places.fact: The shredded remains of a massive star whose light from the explosion reached Earth around the 1660s, though nobody is known to have seen it. JWST sees its debris as knots of orange and pink, a shock front ahead of it, and a curious green curtain nicknamed the Green Monster.
places.type: supernova remnant · the youngest known from a massive star
readout: 11,000 light-years · about 10 light-years across
its debris still flies outward at up to 14,000 km/s

places.name: WR 124
places.fact: A star 30 times the Sun's mass in its last brief, violent stage, throwing off its outer layers. The ejected gas cools into clumps of dust that JWST sees glowing in infrared, ten light-years across.
places.type: Wolf-Rayet star shedding its skin · JWST
readout: 15,000 to 21,000 light-years (estimates differ) · its gas flies out at ~700 km/s
it will probably end as a supernova

places.name: Southern Ring Nebula
places.fact: Shells of gas thrown off by a dying star, layer after layer. The faint star at the centre, not the bright one beside it, made the nebula; JWST showed for the first time that it is wrapped in dust.
places.type: planetary nebula · NGC 3132 · JWST
readout: 2,500 light-years · about half a light-year across
the ejected shells are spaced by the thousands of years between puffs

places.name: Bubble Nebula
places.fact: The wind of a single star about 45 times the Sun's mass, blowing at 1,700 km/s, has inflated a bubble seven light-years wide in the gas around it. The star sits off-centre because the cloud is denser on one side.
places.type: wind-blown bubble · NGC 7635
readout: 7,100 light-years · the bubble is 7 light-years wide
its star, BD+60 2522, is about 45 times the Sun's mass

places.name: the Pleiades
places.fact: About a thousand young stars born together some 100 to 125 million years ago. Their brightest members light up a dust cloud the cluster happens to be passing through, in streaks of blue.
places.type: young star cluster · the Seven Sisters · M45
readout: 444 light-years · about 115 million years old
the dust is not left over from their birth: they are drifting through it

places.name: Einstein Cross
places.fact: Four images of one quasar, whose light set out about 10 billion years ago, arranged around the core of a galaxy far nearer to us. The galaxy's gravity bends the quasar's light along four paths. Seen from anywhere but here, the cross would fall apart.
places.type: a quasar split into four by gravity · Q2237+030
readout: the four images are 1.8 arcseconds apart as seen from Earth
the quasar's light took about 10 billion years to get here

places.name: Boötes Void
places.fact: A roughly spherical hole in the cosmic web some 330 to 400 million light-years across. A region that size would normally hold thousands of galaxies; this one holds about sixty. From its middle, beyond the stars of your own galaxy, you would see almost no other galaxies.
places.type: one of the largest empty regions known
readout: 700 million light-years · 330 to 400 million light-years across
about 60 galaxies, where thousands would be expected

places.name: El Gordo
places.fact: Two giant clusters of galaxies smashing together, together weighing about 3 million billion Suns. The collision heats its gas to about 170 million °C and drives shock waves that glow in radio at both ends.
places.type: colliding galaxy clusters · the fat one
places.where: light left it 7 billion years ago · now ~10 billion light-years away
readout: about 3 million billion times the Sun's mass
we see it as it was when the universe was half its age

places.name: Tabby's Star
places.fact: Kepler saw this star dim irregularly, once by 22%, with no pattern a planet could make. Its light dims more in blue than in red, the signature of fine dust: most likely uneven clouds of it, perhaps from shattered comets or moons.
places.type: the star with mysterious dips · KIC 8462852
readout: 1,470 light-years · dips of up to 22% lasting days
the dust clouds are drawn where they could be; nobody has seen them

places.name: Comet Hale-Bopp
places.fact: Found in July 1995 by Alan Hale and Thomas Bopp, it became one of the brightest comets of the last century, visible to the naked eye for about 18 months, a record. Its nucleus is about 60 km across, several times bigger than most.
places.type: the great comet of 1997 · C/1995 O1
readout: shown as on 1 April 1997, at its closest to the Sun (0.91 AU)
now 51.3 AU out, dark and frozen · back in about 2,500 years

places.name: Comet NEOWISE
places.fact: Found by NASA's NEOWISE space telescope on 27 March 2020, it became a naked-eye comet with a long curved dust tail in July 2020. Its nucleus is about 5 km across.
places.type: the bright comet of July 2020 · C/2020 F3
readout: shown as on 3 July 2020, at its closest to the Sun (0.29 AU)
it passed Earth at 103 million km on 23 July · now 18.9 AU out
back in about 6,800 years

places.name: Comet Tsuchinshan-ATLAS
places.fact: Found by China's Purple Mountain Observatory in January 2023, and on its own by the ATLAS survey in February. In mid-October 2024 Earth passed through the plane of its orbit, and dust spread along that orbit showed as a thin spike pointing toward the Sun: an anti-tail.
places.type: the bright comet of October 2024 · C/2023 A3
readout: shown as on 14 October 2024, two days after it passed Earth at 70 million km
now 8.89 AU out, on a path that may leave the Solar System

places.name: 3I/ATLAS
places.fact: Found on 1 July 2025 by the ATLAS survey telescope in Chile: only the third object known to come from another star. It swept past the Sun just inside the orbit of Mars and is heading back into interstellar space; its speed hints that it may be older than the Solar System.
places.type: the third interstellar object · a comet from another star
readout: shown as on 29 October 2025, at its closest to the Sun (1.36 AU), moving at 68 km/s
now 13.2 AU out, leaving at about 58 km/s
nucleus between 0.44 and 5.6 km across (Hubble)

places.name: Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko
places.fact: The comet ESA's Rosetta orbited from 2014 to 2016, and the first one landed on (by Philae, on 12 November 2014). Two lobes 4.1 and 2.6 km long, joined by a neck like a rubber duck, and about half as dense as water.
places.type: Rosetta's comet · the rubber duck
readout: shown as on 13 August 2015, at its closest to the Sun (1.24 AU)
then losing up to 300 kg of water and 1,000 kg of dust a second
now 4.35 AU from the Sun · it circles it every 6.4 years

places.name: Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9
places.fact: Jupiter's gravity tore this comet into about 21 pieces in July 1992. Two years later, from 16 to 22 July 1994, they hit Jupiter one after another at 60 km/s: the first collision between two Solar System bodies ever watched.
places.type: the comet that hit Jupiter in July 1994 · replayed
readout: a replay of July 1994, sped up
the biggest pieces hit with the energy of tens of thousands of megatons of TNT
plumes rose 3,000 km; the dark scars were about the size of Earth

places.name: Kreutz sungrazers
places.fact: Pieces of one giant comet that broke up centuries ago, still on nearly the same orbit, which skims the Sun's corona as close as about 130,000 km above its surface. The SOHO spacecraft has found over 4,000 of them; most are only a few metres to tens of metres across and boil away.
places.type: a family of comets that dive through the Sun's corona · replayed
readout: a replay, 15,000 times faster than real · perihelion 1.2 Sun radii from its centre
closest to the Sun they move at over 500 km/s
famous members: the Great Comets of 1843 and 1882, Ikeya-Seki (1965), Lovejoy (2011)

places.name: the Perseids
places.fact: Every August Earth runs through the dust shed by Comet Swift-Tuttle, whose nucleus is 26 km across. The grains, mostly the size of sand, hit the air at 59 km/s and burn up as shooting stars 80 to 120 km up.
places.type: meteor shower in August · dust from Comet Swift-Tuttle
readout: the dust stream along Comet Swift-Tuttle's orbit (spread drawn illustratively)
Earth crosses it around 12 August · up to about 100 meteors an hour
the comet returns every 133 years, next in 2126

places.name: the Leonids
places.fact: Comet Tempel-Tuttle, 3.6 km across, returns every 33 years and leaves fresh trails of dust; when Earth hits one, the November Leonids become a storm, as in 1966, when thousands of meteors a minute fell over the western US. At about 70 km/s they are the fastest of the big yearly showers.
places.type: meteor shower in November · dust from Comet Tempel-Tuttle
readout: the dust stream along Comet Tempel-Tuttle's orbit (spread drawn illustratively)
Earth crosses it around 17 November · about 15 meteors an hour in most years
the densest dust trails close to the comet bring the storms

places.name: Vesta
places.fact: The second-heaviest body in the asteroid belt, a squashed ball about 525 km across. A giant impact dug Rheasilvia, a crater about 500 km wide around its south pole, and left a mountain in the middle about 22 km high. NASA's Dawn orbited Vesta in 2011 and 2012.
places.type: asteroid · the brightest asteroid in our sky
readout: 2.49 AU from the Sun · 573 x 557 x 446 km
Rheasilvia is 505 km wide; its central peak rises about 22 km

places.name: Bennu
places.fact: A loose pile of rubble about 500 m wide, shaped like a spinning top, with a ridge round its middle and boulders everywhere. NASA's OSIRIS-REx scooped up 121.6 g of it and dropped the sample off at Earth on 24 September 2023. It has a 1 in 2,700 chance of hitting Earth in 2182.
places.type: near-Earth asteroid · a spinning top of rubble
readout: 1.35 AU from the Sun · 505 x 492 x 457 m
one turn every 4.3 hours · one lap of the Sun every 437 days

places.name: 51 Pegasi b
places.fact: Found in 1995 by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, who shared half of the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics for it. A gas giant about half Jupiter's mass, it circles its star every 4.2 days, far closer than Mercury is to the Sun.
places.type: the first planet found around a Sun-like star · Dimidium
readout: orbit 4.2 days (sped up here) at 0.05 AU · 50.6 light-years
seen from Earth it never crosses its star, so its width is unknown: drawn Jupiter-sized, colours a guess

places.name: K2-18 b
places.fact: A world 2.6 times Earth's width and 8.6 times its mass, orbiting where its star's warmth could allow liquid water. In 2023 JWST found methane and carbon dioxide in its hydrogen-rich air, and it may hide a deep ocean. A claimed hint of dimethyl sulfide, a gas that on Earth comes only from living things, has not been confirmed, and it can also form without life.
places.type: sub-Neptune in the habitable zone · studied by JWST
readout: orbit 33 days (sped up here) at 0.16 AU · 124 light-years
JWST measured its gases, not its looks: the colours are a guess

places.name: HD 189733 b
places.fact: A gas giant a little bigger than Jupiter. In 2013 Hubble measured its colour: deep blue, probably from a haze of tiny silicate grains, the stuff of sand and glass. Its day side is over 1,000 °C, and winds of several thousand km/h may blow that glass sideways as rain.
places.type: the deep blue planet · it may rain glass
readout: orbit 2.2 days (sped up here) at 0.031 AU · 64.5 light-years
Hubble measured its blue; the cloud bands are drawn

places.name: Gaia BH3
places.fact: A black hole 33 times the Sun's mass, 1,926 light-years away in Aquila: the heaviest found in our galaxy that was made by a star. It gives off no light; Gaia found it in 2024 from the wobble of an ancient giant star that circles it every 11.6 years.
places.type: dormant black hole · 33 Suns · the heaviest known that formed from a star in our galaxy
readout: event horizon about 195 km across · 33 times the Sun's mass
its star swings between 4.5 and 28.6 AU from it (the orbit is sped up here)

places.name: T Coronae Borealis
places.fact: A red giant and a white dwarf, 3,000 light-years away. About every 80 years, gas that the white dwarf has pulled off the giant explodes on the dwarf's surface, and for a few days the pair can be seen without a telescope. It erupted in 1866 and 1946, and astronomers expect the next eruption soon.
places.type: recurrent nova · the Blaze Star
readout: the two stars circle each other every 228 days (shown ~18 s)
last erupted in 1946 · the replay here comes every 34 s

places.name: Lagoon Nebula
places.fact: A cloud of glowing hydrogen about 110 by 50 light-years, where new stars are forming. A lane of dark dust across it gives it its name. On one side of the dark lane the young star Herschel 36 lights up the Hourglass; the young cluster NGC 6530 sits on the other.
places.type: star-forming region · M8 · in Sagittarius
readout: about 4,300 light-years (Gaia measured its cluster) · 110 x 50 light-years
faintly visible to the naked eye from a dark site

places.name: Great Hercules Cluster
places.fact: Several hundred thousand stars in a ball about 145 light-years across, around 12 billion years old. In 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope beamed a short message toward it. Travelling at the speed of light, it will take about 25,000 years to get there.
places.type: globular cluster · M13, target of the Arecibo message
readout: about 25,000 light-years · 145 light-years across
the Arecibo message has covered 51 light-years of the way so far

places.name: Dumbbell Nebula
places.fact: The first planetary nebula ever found, by Charles Messier in 1764: the outer layers of a dying Sun-like star, blown off over the last 10,000 years or so. From Earth its brightest gas looks like an apple core.
places.type: planetary nebula · M27 · in Vulpecula
readout: 1,260 light-years (Gaia) · about 3 light-years across
its central star is over 100,000 °C

places.name: Owl Nebula
places.fact: A round shell of gas thrown off by a dying star some 10,000 years ago. Two darker patches inside it look like an owl's eyes: they are the two ends of one barrel-shaped hollow in the shell, tilted about 45 degrees to our view.
places.type: planetary nebula · M97 · in Ursa Major
readout: 2,660 light-years (Gaia) · about 2.6 light-years across
the eyes are the ends of one tilted hollow, not two holes

places.name: Trifid Nebula
places.fact: Three kinds of nebula in one: a red cloud of glowing hydrogen, split into three lobes by dark lanes of dust, and a blue cloud of dust beside it that only reflects starlight. A young, very hot star at its middle lights it up.
places.type: star-forming region · M20 · in Sagittarius
readout: 4,100 light-years (Gaia) · about 35 light-years across
its dark lanes are dust in front of the glowing gas

places.name: Omega Nebula
places.fact: One of the brightest star-forming regions in our galaxy. Its brightest gas forms a bar with a hook at one end, a swan or a Greek omega. Massive young stars inside are eating into the dark cloud beside it, where new stars are still forming.
places.type: star-forming region · M17 · the Swan · in Sagittarius
readout: 5,500 light-years (Gaia) · its bright part about 20 light-years across
its central stars are only about a million years old

places.name: Beehive Cluster
places.fact: Over a thousand stars born together some 600 to 700 million years ago. Known since ancient times as a little cloud, it was seen as stars by Galileo in 1610. Planets have been found round several of its stars.
places.type: open star cluster · M44 · Praesepe · in Cancer
readout: 600 light-years (Gaia) · its stars spread over about 40 light-years
about 650 million years old · 600 of its stars as Gaia measured them

places.name: Wild Duck Cluster
places.fact: One of the richest and most massive open clusters known: thousands of stars born together about 300 million years ago. Its brightest stars form a V, like a flight of wild ducks.
places.type: open star cluster · M11 · in Scutum
readout: 7,300 light-years (Gaia) · its stars spread over about 35 light-years
about 300 million years old · 600 of its stars as Gaia measured them

places.name: Ptolemy's Cluster
places.fact: A bright cluster by the tail of Scorpius, easy to see with the naked eye and the farthest south of all the Messier objects. Ptolemy described it nearly 1,900 years ago as a nebula following the sting of Scorpius.
places.type: open star cluster · M7 · in Scorpius
readout: 900 light-years (Gaia) · its stars spread over about 45 light-years
about 220 million years old · 600 of its stars as Gaia measured them

places.name: M3
places.fact: Some 400,000 Suns' worth of stars about 11 billion years old, and the first object in his catalogue that Messier discovered himself (1764). It holds about 240 RR Lyrae stars, more than almost any other globular cluster, each brightening and fading every half a day or so.
places.type: globular cluster · in Canes Venatici
readout: 33,200 light-years · about 170 light-years across
about 240 of its stars pulse in brightness

places.name: M4
places.fact: The nearest globular cluster to us, about 12 billion years old. Hubble found some of the oldest white dwarfs known in it, and its one known pulsar has a planet, among the oldest planets known.
places.type: globular cluster · the nearest · in Scorpius
readout: 6,000 light-years · about 55 light-years across
its pulsar's planet probably formed 12 to 13 billion years ago

places.name: M22
places.fact: Probably the first globular cluster ever found, in 1665, and one of the brightest in our sky. Radio telescopes found two black holes inside it in 2012, and it hides a small planetary nebula.
places.type: globular cluster · in Sagittarius
readout: 10,800 light-years · about 100 light-years across
about 470,000 times the Sun's mass in all

places.name: Sunflower Galaxy
places.fact: A spiral without long, clear arms: its stars and dust lie in many short arm segments, like the seeds of a sunflower. A faint loop of stars round it is all that is left of a small galaxy it swallowed.
places.type: flocculent spiral galaxy · M63 · in Canes Venatici
readout: 29 million light-years · about 100,000 light-years across
its arms are many short pieces, not two long ones

places.name: Black Eye Galaxy
places.fact: A dark band of dust sweeps across one side of its bright centre, like a black eye. Its outer gas turns the opposite way to its inner gas and stars, probably a sign that it took in gas from a small galaxy long ago.
places.type: spiral galaxy · M64 · in Coma Berenices
readout: 14 million light-years · about 43,000 light-years across
its outer gas turns the other way round

places.name: Southern Pinwheel Galaxy
places.fact: A bright, nearly face-on barred spiral, crowded with pink star-forming regions. Astronomers have seen six supernovae explode in it since 1923, among the most for any galaxy.
places.type: barred spiral galaxy · M83 · in Hydra
readout: 15.6 million light-years · about 60,000 light-years across
six supernovae seen in it since 1923

places.name: M77
places.fact: One of the best-known Seyfert galaxies, whose centres blaze with gas falling into a black hole: here one of about 10 million Suns, hidden behind a ring of dust. In 2022 the IceCube detector at the South Pole found evidence of neutrinos coming from it.
places.type: spiral galaxy with an active centre · in Cetus
readout: 35 million light-years (Cepheids; older estimates go up to 47)
about 60,000 light-years across · a black hole of about 10 million Suns
