places.name: M65
places.fact: One of three spirals close together in Leo, the Leo Triplet. Its arms are wound tightly and it has little gas left, so it forms few new stars now.
places.type: spiral galaxy · the Leo Triplet · in Leo
readout: 37 million light-years · about 80,000 light-years across
M66 is about 220,000 light-years from it on the sky

places.name: M66
places.fact: The brightest of the Leo Triplet. Its arms are lopsided, probably stirred by a close pass with its neighbour NGC 3628 about 800 million years ago.
places.type: barred spiral galaxy · the Leo Triplet · in Leo
readout: 36 million light-years · about 105,000 light-years across
five possible supernovae seen in it since 1973

places.name: M106
places.fact: Water molecules swirling round its central black hole shine as natural masers. Tracking them gave its distance by pure geometry, the first such distance to a galaxy beyond our Local Group. Two extra arms of hot gas, seen in radio and X-rays, mark where jets from its black hole heat the gas in its disc.
places.type: spiral galaxy · in Canes Venatici
readout: 24.7 million light-years, measured geometrically from its masers
about 120,000 light-years across · a black hole of about 40 million Suns

places.name: Phantom Galaxy
places.fact: A textbook spiral seen almost exactly face-on, its two long arms traced by pink star-forming regions. It is faint for a Messier object, hence the name. JWST's 2022 picture showed its dust as a lace of filaments.
places.type: grand-design spiral galaxy · M74 · in Pisces
readout: 32 million light-years · about 90,000 light-years across
seen almost face-on, tilted about 10 to 20 degrees

places.name: M84
places.fact: A big, smooth galaxy near the heart of the Virgo Cluster, at the start of the curved line of galaxies called Markarian's Chain. Its central black hole of about 850 million Suns fires two jets that show in radio light.
places.type: elliptical galaxy · Markarian's Chain · Virgo Cluster
readout: 60 million light-years · about 125,000 light-years across
its black hole weighs about 850 million Suns

places.name: M86
places.fact: One of the few galaxies coming toward us. It falls through the Virgo Cluster toward us at about 1,300 km/s, faster than the cluster itself moves away from us, so its light is shifted to the blue. Its hot gas streams off behind it in a long plume.
places.type: lenticular galaxy · Markarian's Chain · Virgo Cluster
readout: 58.3 million light-years · about 150,000 light-years across
coming toward us at about 240 km/s

places.name: Little Dumbbell Nebula
places.fact: One of the faintest objects in Messier's list, found by Pierre Méchain in 1780 and given two NGC numbers because it was thought to be two clouds side by side. A ring of gas seen nearly edge-on makes the bright bar, and two faint lobes of gas are blown out on either side of it.
places.type: planetary nebula · M76 · in Perseus
readout: about 3,400 light-years (uncertain by about 40%) · about 2.6 light-years across
its central star is about 140,000 to 210,000 °C

places.name: M78
places.fact: A cloud of dust that shines only by the light of a close pair of young, hot stars at its head, scattered back toward us and mostly blue. Dozens of young stars, some firing jets, are forming in and around it.
places.type: reflection nebula · in Orion
readout: 1,320 light-years (Gaia) · about 3 light-years across
it shines almost only by light it scatters

places.name: Sagittarius Star Cloud
places.fact: Not a cluster but a window: a gap in the dust of our galaxy through which we see a crowd of stars far off toward its inner parts. Dark clouds of dust such as Barnard 92 hang in front of it, and the open cluster NGC 6603 is seen within it.
places.type: star cloud · M24 · in Sagittarius
readout: its stars are about 10,000 to 16,000 light-years away
about 300 light-years across · a gap in the dust toward the inner galaxy

places.name: Butterfly Cluster
places.fact: Its brightest stars outline a butterfly with open wings. Most are hot and blue-white, but the brightest, BM Scorpii, is an orange giant; on the sky it is the Messier object nearest the centre of our galaxy.
places.type: open star cluster · M6 · in Scorpius
readout: 1,470 light-years (Gaia) · its stars spread over about 30 light-years
50 to 80 million years old · 533 of its stars as Gaia measured them

places.name: M23
places.fact: A rich, scattered cluster in the Milky Way's band in Sagittarius, found by Messier in 1764. Over a thousand of its stars have been picked out by their shared motion.
places.type: open star cluster · in Sagittarius
readout: 2,330 light-years (Gaia) · its stars spread over about 45 light-years
about 300 million years old · 600 of its stars as Gaia measured them

places.name: M25
places.fact: A bright cluster you can see without a telescope from a dark site. One of its stars, U Sagittarii, is a Cepheid: it swells and shrinks, brightening and fading every 6.7 days, and helps set the scale of distances in space.
places.type: open star cluster · in Sagittarius
readout: 2,100 light-years (Gaia) · its stars spread over about 50 light-years
about 100 million years old · 565 of its stars as Gaia measured them

places.name: M29
places.fact: A small, young cluster of hot stars in Cygnus, dimmed several times over by the dust between us. Its brightest stars form a small box with a little triangle above it, a shape nicknamed the Cooling Tower.
places.type: open star cluster · in Cygnus
readout: 5,600 light-years (Gaia) · its stars spread over about 40 light-years
about 10 million years old · 70 of its stars as Gaia measured them

places.name: M34
places.fact: A bright, loose cluster in Perseus, just visible to the naked eye from a dark site. Its stars are about 220 million years old, a stage between the young Pleiades and the older Hyades; how fast its stars spin gives a matching age.
places.type: open star cluster · in Perseus
readout: 1,600 light-years (Gaia) · its stars spread over about 40 light-years
about 220 million years old · 589 of its stars as Gaia measured them

places.name: M35
places.fact: A big, bright cluster at the feet of Gemini, about the size of the full Moon on the sky. The small, dimmer cluster NGC 2158 beside it is about four times farther away and about ten times older.
places.type: open star cluster · in Gemini
readout: 2,740 light-years (Gaia) · its stars spread over about 50 light-years
about 150 million years old · 600 of its stars as Gaia measured them

places.name: M36
places.fact: The youngest of the three bright clusters in Auriga: hot blue stars with no red giants yet. About eight times closer, it would look much like the Pleiades.
places.type: open star cluster · in Auriga
readout: 3,670 light-years (Gaia) · its stars spread over about 20 light-years
about 27 million years old · 217 of its stars as Gaia measured them

places.name: M37
places.fact: The richest of the three bright clusters in Auriga, with thousands of stars; about a dozen of them have swollen into red giants. It even holds a planetary nebula, one of only a handful known in an open cluster.
places.type: open star cluster · in Auriga
readout: 4,570 light-years (Gaia) · its stars spread over about 40 light-years
about 500 million years old · 600 of its stars as Gaia measured them

places.name: M38

places.name: the Halo
places.fact: A long-range cruiser from a civilisation that learned to fold space. Seen from above it is a trident: a needle-shaped bow and two crescent arms sweeping back to the engines at their tips. It roams round the wonders of the universe, a couple of minutes at each, then moves on: light speed for short hops, a fold through space for long ones. At each place it does a job or two: a sensor scan, a weapons test, a skim through a gas giant or a star, or an outing by Pip, its little drone.
